title: Hugging Face on AMD Instinct MI455X: First Transformers Results
gist: Hugging Face got early access to AMD's new Instinct MI455X (432 GB HBM4, up to 23.3 TB/s bandwidth, vs 192 GB on MI300) and reports first Transformers results: ~99.5% pass rate across a 24-model test suite, statistically level with MI300 (99.4%) and an NVIDIA A10 (99.1%), and over 3x more concurrent requests on one accelerator serving Qwen3-32B in BF16. No speed comparison yet — the claim so far is memory capacity and software readiness, not throughput.

insights.claim: AMD's Instinct MI455X, introduced at Advancing AI 2026, carries 432 GB of HBM4 and up to 23.3 TB/s of memory bandwidth per card, versus 192 GB on the prior MI300 generation — a 2.25x capacity jump in one generation.
insights.speaker: Abdennacer Badaoui
insights.so_what: Memory capacity per package is the axis AMD has chosen to compete on against NVIDIA; it directly sets how large a model can be served without multi-GPU sharding.
insights.quote: Each card comes with 432 GB of ultra-fast HBM4 and up to 23.3 TB/s of memory bandwidth.
insights.locator: A First Look at the MI455

insights.claim: A four-accelerator MI455X system exposes roughly 1.7 TB of high-bandwidth memory in a single machine, letting larger models stay on fewer devices and giving long-context workloads more room for KV cache.
insights.speaker: Abdennacer Badaoui
insights.so_what: Fewer devices per model means less interconnect dependency — the one place NVIDIA's NVLink advantage matters least is a workload that fits in one node.
insights.locator: The most immediate change from the previous generation

insights.claim: Hugging Face argues the practical constraint in AI serving is memory rather than compute, since serving systems can only keep more requests active until memory becomes the limiting factor.
insights.speaker: Abdennacer Badaoui
insights.so_what: If memory is the binding constraint in inference economics, HBM capacity — not FLOPS — is the right metric for comparing accelerator TCO.
insights.quote: serving systems can keep more requests active before memory becomes the limiting factor
insights.locator: It means larger models can stay on fewer devices

insights.claim: In a fixed-model capacity test, a single 432 GB MI455X supported over three times more concurrent requests than a 192 GB MI300 before running out of memory, driven by a roughly 3x larger KV cache after loading a 64 GB Qwen3-32B BF16 model.
insights.speaker: Abdennacer Badaoui
insights.so_what: Concurrency per accelerator is the direct driver of cost-per-token in inference serving; a 3x gain on the same model class is a real unit-economics argument for AMD.
insights.quote: the 432 GB MI455X supported over three times more concurrent requests before reaching its own limit
insights.locator: To make that concrete, we ran a preliminary capacity study

insights.claim: Hugging Face explicitly has not yet run speed comparisons on the MI455X, so the published evidence covers capacity and test-suite health only, not throughput or latency versus NVIDIA parts.
insights.speaker: Abdennacer Badaoui
insights.so_what: The most decision-relevant number for buyers is still missing; treat the MI455X narrative as unresolved until a tokens/sec comparison lands.
insights.quote: We will follow-up with speed comparison as we progress with our tests.
insights.locator: We will follow-up with speed comparison

insights.claim: Across Hugging Face's curated 24-architecture Transformers test suite, MI455X passes at approximately 99.5%, essentially matching the 99.4% measured on MI300 and beating the 99.1% measured on an NVIDIA A10 in daily CI.
insights.speaker: Abdennacer Badaoui
insights.so_what: The historical objection to AMD accelerators was software maturity, not silicon; parity on a mainstream framework test suite at launch erodes that objection.
insights.quote: the MI455 success rate across these 24 models is approximately 99.5%, depending on a handful of flaky tests

insights.claim: Hugging Face treats pass rate on a curated 24-model suite spanning encoders, decoders, vision, audio, multimodal and modern LLMs as its main bring-up signal for a new accelerator, calling it a proxy for broader ecosystem health.
insights.speaker: Abdennacer Badaoui
insights.so_what: A reusable, publicly checkable yardstick for judging whether any non-NVIDIA accelerator is actually usable, rather than relying on vendor MLPerf submissions.
insights.locator: When we bring up a new accelerator in Transformers

insights.claim: Reaching that pass rate required cross-stack work with AMD: enabling a stable Flash Attention path, adding torchcodec support for audio and video in multimodal models, and resolving output-comparison discrepancies found in testing.
insights.speaker: Abdennacer Badaoui
insights.so_what: Day-one parity was engineered by a joint team, not inherited — the moat is the ongoing co-engineering relationship, which is fragile if either side deprioritizes it.
insights.locator: Reaching this level required work across the stack

insights.claim: Transformers already runs daily CI on MI300 infrastructure and Hugging Face is expanding coverage in 2026 to AMD Ryzen and Radeon systems, extending the partnership from datacenter parts down to client silicon.
insights.speaker: Abdennacer Badaoui
insights.so_what: Client-side coverage points at local/edge inference on AMD consumer hardware — an under-modelled second front against NVIDIA's consumer GPU install base.

insights.claim: Hugging Face is working with AMD's AITER team to publish optimized AMD kernels on the Hugging Face Kernel Hub so they can be consumed directly in Transformers workflows.
insights.speaker: Abdennacer Badaoui
insights.so_what: Distributing vendor kernels through a neutral hub lowers the switching cost off CUDA — the mechanism by which AMD's software gap actually closes.
insights.locator: At the kernel level, we're also working with the AITER team

insights.claim: Next steps are adding MI455 to the Transformers CI, bringing more AITER kernels to the Kernel Hub, and expanding MI455 validation across additional Hugging Face libraries beyond Transformers.
insights.speaker: Abdennacer Badaoui
insights.so_what: MI455 entering permanent CI is the checkpoint that turns an early-access demo into supported infrastructure — watch for that announcement as the real adoption signal.

insights.claim: AMD granted Hugging Face pre-launch access to MI455X specifically so validation results could be published on day one alongside the hardware announcement.
insights.speaker: Abdennacer Badaoui
insights.so_what: AMD is treating open-source ecosystem endorsement as a launch asset, indicating it knows software credibility — not specs — is what gates its datacenter share.
insights.quote: Thanks again to the AMD team for giving us early access and the close collaboration needed to have those results on day one!
